questions.prompt: A company breaches a leverage covenant but has made every payment on time. What is its position?
choices: Nothing happens until a payment is actually missed
It is in default, and negotiating leverage has shifted to its lenders
The loan automatically converts to equity
The covenant is waived by law if payments are current
questions.explanation: Covenant breach is a default in its own right. What follows is usually a negotiation, but the sponsor now needs something from lenders, and lenders charge for it.

questions.prompt: EBITDA falls 20% while debt is unchanged. What happens to the leverage ratio?
choices: It is unchanged, because no new debt was raised
It falls, because the company is smaller
It rises mechanically, because the denominator shrank
It depends entirely on the interest rate
questions.explanation: Leverage is debt divided by EBITDA. A fall in EBITDA raises the ratio without any new borrowing — which is how covenants are breached in a downturn.

questions.prompt: What did the spread of covenant-lite lending change about how leveraged companies fail?
choices: It eliminated defaults by removing the tests that trigger them
It removed the quarterly early-warning system, so problems surface later and larger
It shifted all risk to equity holders and away from lenders
questions.explanation: Without maintenance covenants, deterioration is not flagged each quarter. Defaults become less frequent but arrive later and worse, typically at a missed payment or an unrefinanceable maturity.

questions.prompt: A structure financed with floating-rate debt can come under serious strain from interest rate rises alone, with no change in the business.
questions.explanation: True. A floating rate resets with the benchmark, so the interest bill on a structure sized in a low-rate environment can rise materially while operations are unchanged.

questions.prompt: Trace how a leveraged company gets from a single bad quarter to a debt-for-equity restructuring, and name two structural choices that would have made it more resilient.
rubric: Starts with the trigger: EBITDA falls through lost demand, cost inflation or customer loss
Explains that leverage rises mechanically as the denominator shrinks, breaching or threatening a covenant
Describes cash being diverted to debt service, with capex and marketing cut in ways that worsen the underlying business
Describes refinancing becoming expensive or unavailable from a position of visible weakness, leading to a debt-for-equity swap that wipes out the sponsor's equity
Names at least two protections — genuine leverage headroom, fixed or hedged rates, long maturities, or a business whose revenue holds up in a downturn — and notes each costs return in the good case
